catalog_quote: Position and Representation of Accent. Accented vowels are produced with an anterior tensing of the vocal folds and larynx, causing a raised pitch on the accented vowel. Accent is indicated by ʹ before a vowel in K. and V., the two languages in which accentual position is distinctive. Compare the position of accent in each row: [column Kâmkata.kâmviri:] ʹâćaň 'come!' [plural] ... âćʹaň 'carry on your backs!' [plural]; [column Kâmkata.kâmviri:] ʹu tia 'stand up!' ... utʹia 'wait!'; [column Vâsi.ṣupu:] ʹimi 'wife's brother' ... irʹi 'co-wife'. In K. and V. accent is alternatively represented positionally before the word that bears it. The three positional possibilities of accent placement in K.km are initial-syllable, indicated by `, second-syllable, indicated by ^, and final-syllable, indicated by ´. ... Note also final-stressed accent in K.km, found only in loanwords ... In the remaining languages (including Tr.?) accent falls automatically on a word's final syllable (excluding inflectional or enclitic suffixes) and is not written. [Iranica 2010, Phonology:] Accent is indicated by ' before a vowel in K. and V., where it is phonemic. In the remaining groups (including Tr.?) accent apparently falls automatically on the last syllable of a word's stem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In Vâsi-vari (Prasun), as in Kâmkata-vari, the position of the word accent (realised as raised pitch on the accented vowel) is distinctive/phonemic and must be marked lexically (e.g. ṣupu-dialect ʹimi 'wife's brother' vs irʹi 'co-wife'); this contrasts with the other Nuristani languages, where accent falls automatically on the stem-final syllable. Comparative evidence (Halfmann 2025: 97, 56) indicates that Prasun stress generally sits on the syllable continuing the Indo-Iranian penult, which after loss of final syllables is very often the synchronic word-final syllable (žičí, piždá; village names uṣʹüt, ṣupʹu, üšʹüt), so the system looks like lexical accent with a strong final-syllable tendency; the modern reference grammar reportedly calls the stress system not yet well understood (Buddruss & Degener 2017: 62, cited by Halfmann 2024).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Vâsi-vari; Strand notes final-syllable accent in Kâmviri loanwords only for K.km. Halfmann 2025 notes Prasun syncopes concentrate in pre-stress (antepenultimate) position.
new_statements.domain_note: Strand's statements concern word-level accent (pitch prominence) in citation forms, marked before the vowel; for the non-distinctive languages the domain is the stem (inflectional/enclitic suffixes excluded). Strand 2019 adds that accent produces sub-phonemic vowel lengthening in Vâsi-vari. Morgenstierne 1949: 205 (snippets only) has a 'Stress.' section noting 'Stressed final vowels were usually noted as long' and that his 'notation of stress is not always consistent'.
new_statements.identity_note: Strand's 'V.' = Vâsi-vari, the autonym-based name for Prasun/Pārūni/Wasi-weri (pras1239, ISO prn); his contrastive accent pair is from the ṣupʹu (uppermost village) dialect, and his lexicon index distinguishes three dialects (uṣʹüt-varʹe; üšʹüt-üćʹü-zumʹu-vari; ṣupʹu-varʹi), none with separate Glottolog codes. Buddruss & Degener's Materialien cover the same three dialect groups.

sources.note: Comparative-historical. p. 97: 'though much still remains unclear about Pr. vowel developments, there seem to be no strong parallels for a syncope of the Indo-Iranian penultimate syllable in Pr., which synchronically in fact generally bears the stress (e.g., žičí 'book, letter; embroidery, carving' < *čitr-i-ta-). Later syncopes instead overwhelmingly show up in pre-stress (antepenultimate) position'. p. 56: 'Word-final stress is attested.. in Pr. piždá bës ‘snowstorm’' (loan from Katë). p. 10: Prasun vowel-length status unclear.

tone.quote: Dameli has de facto been treated as an Indo-Aryan language by recent authors (e.g. Liljegren 2017: 109–111). This practice is based essentially on the following single sentence in Strand (2001a: 254): “The laryngeal processes of this language, including aspiration, tones, and basic laryngeal posture, are characteristically Indo-Aryan, not Nuristani. It is therefore most probably Indo-Aryan in origin.” ... The historical correlation of tone and historical voiced aspirates could not yet be proved for Dameli (cf. Morgenstierne 1942: 125; Perder 2013: 32)
